records.c: Indirect target of the hardware IRQ handler. Each stage schedules the next stage and replaces this pointer.
Set up video, blank the screen with glyph $FD and copy the two prompt lines from $BA0C and $BA26. Wait for the keyboard matrix to read Space, then jump to the first disk-load entry.
Clear the three life sprite pointer slots and fill up to three with pointer 7 according to $25D4.
Clear the playfield, copy the nine glyph codes for GAME OVER, select sound number 7 and wait on the raster.
Nine custom glyph codes for the game-over message.
Compare the three current score bytes with successive table entries. Shift the lower entries and corresponding names down when the score qualifies, then copy the new score and set up the name entry.
Nine eight-glyph slots for the high-score names and entries shifted down by $0899.
Tail of the eight-glyph score-name table, including the destination of the shift from the higher rank.
Nine three-byte BCD score records in high, middle, low order.
Packed decimal middle byte of each score record, the second field within the three-byte stride.
Packed decimal low byte of each score record.
Destination high byte for the three-byte shift into the next lower rank.
Destination middle byte in the next lower rank.
Indexed byte of the destination score entry, three bytes after the corresponding source field.
Initialise the name and selectable-glyph strip. Left and right scroll through 32 choices and fire accepts the focused glyph. Special glyphs delete a character or finish entry.
Fifteen character codes copied to the first line of the high-score name entry screen.
Fifteen character codes copied to the second line of the name entry prompt.
Schedule the next name-entry raster split and apply the horizontal scroll offset at $0D18 to the selector strip.
Clear the fine scroll, schedule the first name-entry split for raster $76, advance the tick and update the music.
Draw 40 glyphs from the selectable character table, wrapping the table index at 32. Highlight the glyph column at $F97C.
Custom glyphs for the selectable name characters, beginning with space. The letter O uses $BD.
Clear the panel, set display colours, then draw the score rows and text into the screen buffer.
Top horizontal frame tiles for the high-score display.
Bottom horizontal frame tiles for the high-score display.
Nine tile codes drawn on the left edge of the high-score frame.
Nine tile codes drawn on the right edge of the high-score frame.
Multiply the row index by four and copy the corresponding ordinal glyphs through the screen pointer at $14.
Multiply the rank in X by eight and copy its saved name glyphs through the screen pointer at $14.
Render the score digits through the custom HUD glyphs.
Eight four-byte ordinal labels, each padded with a custom space, for the high-score table.
Eight editable character codes for the new name, filled by the name-entry loop.
Index of the editable name character, clamped by the eight-character field.
Glyph-table index displayed at the start of the scrolling selector strip.
Fine scroll phase used by the name-entry raster split.
Turn the input in A into the variable glyph at $0D45, clear the playfield and draw the 15-character level-cleared banner. Set sound number 1 and wait before returning.
Fixed-width LEVEL X CLEARED banner with its level digit stored by $0D19.
Patched character in the middle of the level-cleared message.
Clear the screen and draw the continue prompt and its large glyphs. Count down from 9 by waiting on the raster. Return zero for fire and one when the counter expires.
Offsets of the fifteen-cell numeral patterns used in the continue countdown.
Eight custom character codes spelling CONTINUE.
Sixteen character codes instructing the player to press the fire button.
Ten 3-by-5 screen-code patterns for the countdown numeral, read from the indexed offset at $0E17.
Thirteen rows of thirteen screen codes drawn into the centre of the continue panel, with colour 8 for each cell.
Set the shared display state and clear the area used for the centred title and status messages.
Add A to the low BCD score byte and propagate decimal carries through the middle and high bytes. Award a life when the middle byte reaches $10 on a low-byte carry.
Split the packed decimal score into six nibbles and add glyph base $BD before drawing each digit.
Low packed decimal score byte, updated when score is awarded.
Highest packed decimal score byte.
Middle packed decimal score byte. A carry into this field can award an extra life.
Select the keyboard matrix row with $DF and wait for two press-and-release cycles when the column result is $FD. A live P hold reached the comparison with A=$FD.

Count eligible gameplay ticks in a divider reloaded to 50. On rollover decrement the BCD time and enter the death path at expiry. Live instruction stops showed 2:00 becoming 1:59 and 0:00 reaching $1219.
Use the minutes and the two BCD seconds digits to look up four tile bytes per digit. Store them in the two rows of HUD screen RAM.
Countdown minute value, decremented when the BCD seconds roll under zero.
Packed decimal seconds, reset to $59 when borrowing from minutes.
Downcounter reloaded with 50 between timer updates.
Ten tile codes for the upper-left cell of the timer digit.
Upper-right timer cell tile codes for digits 0 through 9.
Lower-left timer cell tile codes for digits 0 through 9.
Lower-right timer cell tile codes for digits 0 through 9.
Copy five rows of the tile-art template to the bottom of screen RAM, set HUD colours and call the time, score and weapon display routines.
Tile codes for the lower panel frame and the four weapon icons. The template starts at screen offset $02F8.
Glyph codes for the bottom line including SCORE and HI with placeholders for both values.
If neither relevant player state byte is set, enter death state 1 and clear the voice-2 effect request before removing type-4 objects from the first three slots.
Clear type-4 objects in slots 0 through 2 and move their Y positions to $FA.
Wait for raster low byte zero and call $10F3 twice per iteration. X gives the iteration count, with initial X=0 performing 256 passes.
Search slots 14 down to 0 for zero entries in $008E,Y. Store the requested number of slot indices starting at $14 and return A=0 on success or A=1 on exhaustion.
Scan $008E through $009C backward. Return the first zero slot in Y, or Y=$FF when all are occupied.

Convert $25D8/$25D9 to tile coordinates, add scroll offsets and fetch the cell from the map at $4000. $277E selects a 512- or 96-byte row stride. Use the cell byte as an index into the table pointed to by $F2 and return its attribute in A.
Add the horizontal and vertical step bytes at $6E,X and $7E,X to the position bytes at $2E,X and $3E,X.
Copy position, shape and colour from the four object arrays into the IRQ's four display arrays for all 16 slots.
Every eighth game tick advance the current sprite pointer. Deactivate the slot at pointer $AC.
Test fifteen object positions against a rectangle around the current slot while the shape index is below $53. Mark overlapping targets and continue into the animation update.
Each eighth tick, advance the shape by four until its pointer reaches $5F. Skip the tick on which it was created.
Alternate the pickup colour and test contact. On collection, start a 100-tick timer that marks eligible objects as hit and then removes the pickup.
Two sprite colours alternated by the raster tick.
On contact, upgrade the active weapon if it is eligible or scan for an upgradeable slot. Clear the temporary contact state, request effect 6 and deactivate the pickup object.
Two flashing colours for the weapon upgrade item.
On contact, add a shadow up to a limit of two. Initialise its slot from the player position and clear its assigned movement history.
Two flashing sprite colours for the shadow item.
Compare the player position with a rectangle 10 horizontal units by 20 vertical units around slot X and enter the death path when inside it.
Every fourth update advance the shape. At the end, remove the slot or replace the yellow variant with one of three pickup types selected by the rolling counter.
Switch slot X to type 6, set its colour and starting shape and request sound 8.
Bit-zero mask used by the shared weapon sprite update to select the alternate colour.
Load the earlier player pose and velocity from the circular history and update the first shadow. Dispatch to the weapon callback with shadow index 1.
Four little-endian action callbacks selected by the even weapon index. Copied to $EC by $2126.
First high byte of the interleaved weapon action pointers read at $2138.
Select the stationary pose if needed, clear both velocities and run the current weapon action as shadow 1.
Read the delayed pose and velocity for the second shadow when allowed by the attack state, then dispatch the current weapon callback with shadow index 2.
Mark slot X inactive and move its Y position below the visible playfield.
Iterate object slots 14 down to 0. Call the target at $F0 for active slots whose object type indexes a nonzero byte in the table at $F6.
Tail-jump through the current weapon-dependent hit-test pointer at $F0.
Build the target rectangle and search all 18 cell-based projectile slots. A matching hit switches the projectile to direction-state $10.
Test the first three cell-based slots, and convert the first overlap to effect coordinates in $2773/$2774 before falling through to the four-slot burst allocator.
Find four inactive objects and assign their positions relative to $2773/$2774. Use the four-entry type and shape tables and return one on allocation failure.
Four horizontal offsets from the effect origin for the component sprites.
Vertical offsets for the same four effect components.
Shape pointers for the four positions in the burst.
Object types for the four component slots.
Establish the target rectangle and check the first three projectile slots for a hit, setting the target’s hit byte when one overlaps.
Work down through the projectile array from Y. Skip inactive slots and compare tile column and row with the four temporary bounds.
Load the object extents and test the three attacker slots. Use separate sword bounds depending on whether $25CE is set and store an object hit on overlap.
Six direction-dependent horizontal sword bounds used when $25CE is clear.
Opposite horizontal edges for those six sword positions.
Six vertical top edges in the ordinary sword rectangle.
Six vertical bottom edges in the ordinary sword rectangle.
Alternative right edges selected by $25CE.
Alternative left edges selected by $25CE.
Alternative top edges selected by $25CE.
Alternative bottom edges selected by $25CE.
Combine the current object position with per-type extents at $F4, $F8 and $FA. Convert the results to tile units for the hit test.
Horizontal step bytes for the airborne movement loop. The direction rules select a four-byte group and the game tick supplies the phase.

Process left and right steering on eighth ticks, choose airborne pose and horizontal step, and test screen limits. On descent, increase downward speed and snap the player onto the floor when the map cell is solid.
Shape pairs used by the airborne loop to select the pose for the facing direction.
Count through the death state and set the grounded or airborne death poses according to time. Use the ground collision check to settle a falling player.
Grounded death pose indexed by the death counter shifted right by five bits.
Airborne death pose selected by the same five-bit shift of the death counter.
Clear the map refresh flag and check player state and ground before processing input. A live Up input reached the jump branch and stepping $190B stored vertical velocity $FD at $008D.
Clear horizontal movement and select a facing-specific display shape.
Four frame values selected by the player tick in the ground movement code.
Ground animation shape values used when there is lateral movement.
Two facing-dependent stationary player shapes.
When any direction is pressed, translate the low CIA joystick bits into an aim index. Increment the weapon tick and dispatch through the installed action pointer at $EC.
Add the weapon sprite and owning actor velocities, then update the weapon sprite colour or shape according to the attack phase.
Start a fire-triggered sword pose using the aim direction and facing. Advance its animation, apply the per-direction nudges and return to the normal pose when the counter reaches 15.
Horizontal movement applied to the actor as the six sword poses start.
Horizontal movement for the mid-frame transition of each sword pose.
Horizontal corrections when each pose finishes.
Six offsets from the owning actor to the optional type-4 weapon sprite.
Vertical offsets from the attacker for the six extended sword positions.
Initial horizontal velocity for an extended sword sprite.
Initial vertical velocity for an extended sword sprite.
Six directional shapes for the optional sword sprite.
Convert the current actor coordinates to a tile column and row, arm its projectile slot and copy the active aim code.
Select the actor’s throwing shape from the aim code. A shape below 9 uses the lower pose base and the rest use the higher base.
On fire, initialise a projectile when the actor’s slot is idle and increase the shared active count before drawing the attack pose.
Check the actor’s two projectile timers when $25D0 permits the extra shot. Stagger the second slot by eight weapon ticks and choose the throwing pose on each launch.
Check two projectile timers at staggered phases. The $25CF mode also starts two neighbouring aim directions at the same position.
Look up the attack direction from the low four, active-low CIA1 input bits.
Column steps indexed by the projectile aim code.
Gate the tile projectile’s horizontal step by a direction-dependent tick mask.
Row steps indexed by the aim code.
Gate the tile projectile’s vertical movement by its aim code.
Maximum reach for the cell-based rope attack, indexed by direction.
Return immediately for the sword, whose attack draws through the sprite pipeline.
Advance the rope’s head, save the covered tile in its restore buffer and draw a blank cell, subject to screen row and column limits.
Restore the saved tile at the current rope endpoint and move the head backward by its directional step.
Convert the rope endpoint to sprite coordinates and choose a directional shape in the type-4 slot. Return when the endpoint is beyond the playable screen.
Process three actor rope slots. Extend, sweep or retract each rope according to its state, maintaining the saved background tiles.
Set the projectile’s drawn tile code to $FC before running the tile movement pass.
Use tile $FE for the other projectile movement path.
Move live tile projectiles using direction, camera movement and tick masks. Save the tile under the new position and put the selected projectile tile there.
Three pointers used when saving and restoring the tiles behind each rope attack.
High byte of the first saved-tile buffer pointer. The reader at $1E53 indexes every other byte.
For weapon selections 2 and 4, restore the tile saved under every active projectile using its current row and column.
High-byte offsets from page $F8 for the tile projectile’s screen row.
Screen address low bytes for 40-column rows beginning at $F800.
Save player history for the shadow figures when moving. Keep the player near the horizontal or vertical scroll threshold, update fine scroll and signal a map refresh when a cell boundary is crossed.
Initialise the player position, shape and facing, clear activity flags and projectiles, and seed active shadows at the starting position.
Install weapon action, screen redraw and hit-test pointers from the selected weapon’s tables, then choose the selected HUD icon colour.
Use the current weapon index to select one five-cell icon address, then set two rows of colour RAM to the requested colour.
Four pointers installed at $EE for the weapon-specific phase called after the map redraw.
High byte of the first interleaved weapon redraw pointer, indexed by the same even selector.
Four pointers installed at $F0 for the shared object hit-test pass.
First high byte in the four two-byte weapon hit-test entries.
The four colour-RAM starting addresses for the weapon icons.
First high byte in the weapon HUD icon pointer list, read when applying the icon colour.
Jump through the current weapon redraw pointer.
Patch the nineteen absolute,Y map loads at $222C and following with the current column and the successive row addresses for a 512-byte map stride.
Copy 19 rows of 40 tile codes from the patched map operands to the visible rows starting at $F800.
Low byte of the mutable source operand for viewport row 1, patched with the camera origin before the 40-cell copy.
High byte of the patched map operand for viewport row 1. The copy loop transfers this row’s forty cells to $F800.

Low byte of the mutable source operand for viewport row 19, patched with the camera origin before the 40-cell copy.
High byte of the patched map operand for viewport row 19. The copy loop transfers this row’s forty cells to $FAD0.
Select VIC bank $C000 through CIA2, turn on multicolour sprites and initialise the screen, scroll and shared colours.
Enable the hardware sprites and call $157D for each of the 16 logical slots.
Mix the two state bytes at $25DC and $25DD through rotates, XOR and add. Store the new low byte at $25DC.
Sample the raster low byte into $25DC and store its doubled value at $25DD, retrying when the doubled result is zero.
Sort the logical sprite indices at $1E by descending Y from $3E using alternating passes from both ends.
Fill the slot-order array with indices 0 through 15 before the sprite pass sorts by Y.
Wait for $11 to differ from the saved tick byte at $09.
Wait until the raster low byte exceeds $C8.
Sample $11 and wait until it changes.
Bank out KERNAL ROM, stop CIA1 timer A, disable the low VIC interrupt enable bits and install the game IRQ and NMI vectors in high RAM.
Save A, X and Y at $02-$04 and dispatch through the current raster handler pointer at $12.
Load the playfield colours and scrolling registers, advance the IRQ tick, and assign the first eight sorted slots to the VIC sprites. Schedule the reuse handler when the next slot needs a sprite.
Wait until a hardware sprite is free, then load its new X, Y, ninth X bit, shape pointer and colour. Schedule the next reuse or the HUD split.
Schedule the HUD pointer update for raster $C1. Acknowledge the raster IRQ and restore the saved registers.
Put sprite shape 3 into all eight pointer slots and schedule the HUD display IRQ for raster $C6.
Set the HUD colours, mode, sprite positions and pointers. Schedule the first playfield interrupt for raster $20 and call both audio update entries before returning.
Seventeen bytes copied to VIC registers $D000-$D010, eight X/Y pairs and the ninth-bit mask.
Base address used for the indexed write of life icon pointers. X starts in the range 1 to 3.
Eight shape pointers copied to $FBF8-$FBFF by the HUD raster handler.
Four HUD shape indices, set to 3 by the reset helper and to $41 on weapon upgrade.
Clear the corresponding hardware sprite's ninth X bit while preserving the other seven.
Set the corresponding hardware sprite's ninth X bit.
Eight-byte effect records supplying envelope, waveform, duration and initial SID frequency fields to $A2CC.
Initial effect 0 descriptor at byte 1, indexed by the effect number times eight.
Initial effect 0 descriptor at byte 2, indexed by the effect number times eight.
Initial effect 0 descriptor at byte 3, indexed by the effect number times eight.
Initial effect 0 descriptor at byte 4, indexed by the effect number times eight.
Initial effect 0 descriptor at byte 5, indexed by the effect number times eight.
Initial effect 0 descriptor at byte 6, indexed by the effect number times eight.
Low initial frequency field, read from each eight-byte effect descriptor before starting that effect.
Parallel eight-byte effect records for the per-tick player, including frequency change and pulse-width state.
Update parameters for effect 0, byte 1 of its second descriptor.
Update parameters for effect 0, byte 2 of its second descriptor.
Packed initial pulse-width fields for each eight-byte effect descriptor. $A317 splits the nibbles for the SID pulse-width registers.
Update parameters for effect 0, byte 4 of its second descriptor.
Update parameters for effect 0, byte 5 of its second descriptor.
Update parameters for effect 0, byte 6 of its second descriptor.
Frequency-high modulation parameter from the second eight-byte effect descriptor. The update paths use it as an XOR mask or as a replacement high byte.
Sparse lookup table mapping effect register offsets 0, 7 and 14 to corresponding music voice indices 0, 1 and 2.
Reset the three effect queues, clear registers $D400–$D417 and set volume 15.
Update three effect voices using X offsets 0, 7 and 14 for the SID register groups.
Decide whether to accept the pending effect on the selected voice. Load its eight-byte descriptors at $A000 and $A100 when starting an effect, then update the voice's frequency and envelope state.
Copy the selected 16-byte tune descriptor at $ACC0 to voice state. Clear the voice indexes, load each initial sequence item and restore master volume.
Bit 7 enables the music update at $A543. Clearing it suppresses further music ticks.
Bit 7 disables the timed fade. In the fade path this byte reloads the counter at $A9F0.
While the tune is active, update its optional volume fade, then advance the three voice tracks and apply note and instrument changes.
Update the current music voice’s modulation phase and move to the next voice. After the final voice, advance the global sequence timing counter.
Read the next sequence control byte through the selected voice's pointer. Interpret repeat, end and fade controls before updating the pattern index and repeat count.
First parameter for each modulation selector from $AC16, copied to $AA79,X.
Second parameter for the same modulation selector, loaded into the channel phase at $AA70,X.
Register offsets 0, 7 and 14 used to select each of the SID’s three seven-register voice groups.
Low bytes of the SID frequency words selected by the seven-bit note value at $A611.
Low-byte pitch values beginning at note index 1.
High bytes of the note frequency words. The index also addresses the low-byte table at $AAA0.
High-byte pitch values beginning at note index 1.
Eight bytes per music instrument. The note player copies the first two bytes to SID envelope registers, reads the control and pulse setup and loads per-note modulation state.

Second line of the startup prompt, copied to the screen at $F9E7.

Patch the pattern to B and enter the common loader.

Bank in KERNAL, blank the screen, silence the SID and prepare drive 8. Set a three-byte wildcard name at $BA68, unpack the file and enter the loaded game at $2780 with ROM banked out again.
The loader passes this three-byte name to SETNAM. The entry wrapper selects its first character and leaves .* as the suffix.
Silence the SID, mask the VIC sources and blank the playfield. Set logical file and name, unpack the file and restore the game's CPU mapping.
Decode literal runs and backward-copy matches from the bitstream. Write both kinds of runs through $FC-$FD, descending toward the packet's final address.
Shift X packed bits from $FB into A and $A7. Refill the bit reservoir through $BC7B when it empties.
Self-modified exit of the refill routine. A normal refill returns to the bit reader; the end-of-packet path unwinds the nested decoder calls.
Shift the next control bit out of $FB. Enter the shared refill when the shift consumes the reservoir's marker bit.
Subtract the run length at $A8 from the unpacker's destination pointer at $FC-$FD.
Configure logical file 8 on drive 8, open the file named through SETNAM and ask the drive to talk. Read a five-byte decoder header into $FB-$FF, then bank out ROM and I/O and enter the unpacker.
Read the five-byte packet header, clear the unused count state and switch out I/O and ROM before decoding the packet.
Temporarily expose the KERNAL and I/O. Update the border counters and packed-byte count, receive one drive byte and restore access to the RAM beneath I/O.
Mutable immediate byte decremented after each serial byte read and used to animate the border.
Preserve the CPU port and border, bank in KERNAL, and start the disk stream through $BC51. When the transfer ends, close the serial stream and restore the saved border and port.
Shared sprite patterns at the beginning of VIC bank $C000. The hardware uses 64-byte slots indexed by the shape pointers written to $FBF8-$FBFF.
Shared sprite slots $10–$1F contain ninja weapon poses, including frames with the blade extended on each side.
Shared slots $20–$2F contain moving weapon poses and small circular or detached effects.
Shared slots $30–$3F hold small shots, the rope weapon's loop and ninja poses swinging above and to the side.
Shared slots $40–$4F contain small rings and projectiles, player poses and early particle effects.
Shared slots $50–$5F hold filled curve shapes, scattered particles and fragmented silhouettes.
Shared slots $60–$6C contain additional particles and humanoid movement poses before the load-specific sprites.
The upper half of the VIC character table selected by $D018=$EE. Codes $A3-$BC supply most of the alphabet, $BD is O and $FD is blank.
Character row data for codes $9E onward. This contains compact HUD patterns followed by the custom alphabet.
